title: TRAM-AI: A Framework for Transparency in Reporting of Medical Imaging Datasets for Artificial Intelligence Development.
desc: [Radiology. Artificial intelligence] Purpose To develop and evaluate TRAM-AI, a consensus-based checklist for verifying whether medical imaging datasets described as publicly accessible are functionally usable for AI development. Materials and Methods A modified Delphi study was conducted. A steering committee generated candidate checklist items through a targeted literature review. An international expert panel (n = 33) rated items on criticality and feasibility across two Delphi rounds. Consensus was defined as ≥ 75% agreement on both dimensions. The checklist was pilot-validated in 10 publicly available datasets. An advisory group of four experts from Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa evaluated cross-regional applicability. Results Of 16 candidate items, 14 were retained in the final checklist; one item was removed because of feasibility concerns, and another was merged with an existing item because of conceptual redundancy. All 14 final items achieved consensus for both criticality and feasibility. The final TRAM-AI checklist comprises 14 items across four domains: Dataset Access and Persistence (3 items), Technical Interoperability (4 items), Metadata and Reproducibility (4 items), and Ethical, Legal, and Maintenance considerations (3 items). In pilot validation, all items were applicable to all 10 datasets, compliance was 90% for trusted repository, de-dentification, and subject-level mapping, 10% for archive validation, and 30% for partition keys. All four advisory group members endorsed the checklist. Conclusion TRAM-AI provides a practical framework for verifying the functional accessibility of medical imaging datasets, complementing existing methodological reporting standards. Further evaluation and broader validation across diverse geographic settings are warranted. ©RSNA, 2026.

title: Advances in Multimodal Artificial Intelligence in Radiology: Data Integration, Foundation Models, and Clinical Applications-A Narrative Review.
desc: [Healthcare (Basel, Switzerland)] Background/Objectives: Multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in radiology to combine medical images with radiology reports, clinical narratives, structured health records, laboratory measurements, and other patient data. These systems may support more context-aware interpretation, reporting, and clinical decision-making than unimodal approaches. This narrative review examines recent technical and clinical advances in multimodal radiology AI and identifies barriers to responsible implementation. Methods: Relevant biomedical and technical literature was identified through targeted searches of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Web of Science, Scopus, arXiv, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar. A documented screening process identified 111 reviewed publications from 1154 records. Study selection and data extraction were conducted by one reviewer without independent verification. Original research, reviews, and commentaries, including selected preprints, were synthesized thematically. Results: The field has progressed from early and late feature fusion toward cross-modal attention, contrastive image-text pretraining, vision-language models, multimodal large language models, and general-purpose foundation models. Applications include diagnostic classification, prognostic modelling, image-text retrieval, visual question answering, clinical decision support, and automated radiology report generation. Despite promising technical results, comparison across studies remains difficult because of heterogeneous datasets, tasks, metrics, and validation designs. Clinical translation is further limited by scarce external and prospective validation, uncertain interpretability, hallucination and omission risks, privacy and fairness concerns, and limited real-world workflow evaluation. Conclusions: Multimodal AI may enable more clinically informed radiological interpretation and reporting, but progress in benchmark performance has outpaced evidence of safety, generalizability, and clinical utility. Future research should prioritize multicentre evaluation, clinically meaningful metrics, transparent reporting, robust safety assessment, and workflow-centred implementation.

title: AI-Assisted Patient Education Before Suturing in Minor Trauma
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Gazi University; conditions: Minor Trauma Requiring Suturing, Pain, Anxiety; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 96; status: RECRUITING] Patients scheduled to undergo suturing for minor trauma in the emergency department frequently experience anticipatory pain and anxiety before the procedure. These experiences may negatively affect perceived pain, cooperation with treatment, adherence, satisfaction, and the overall care experience. However, the realities of emergency department practice, including crowding, high patient volume, staff shortages, and increased workload, may limit effective nurse-patient communication and comprehensive patient education. Patients awaiting suturing for minor trauma often experience uncertainty, prolonged waiting, fear of the procedure, and concern about pain. These factors may increase anxiety, which can further intensify pain perception and negatively influence patients' cooperation with treatment and satisfaction with care. Previous reports indicate that many patients waiting in emergency departments seek information about waiting times, care processes, and their medical conditions, highlighting a substantial need for accessible and reliable information. During this waiting period, patients may increasingly use artificial intelligence-based digital resources to obtain information about their health condition and the procedure they are about to undergo. However, information generated by artificial intelligence may be inaccurate, incomplete, or insufficiently tailored to the clinical context. Therefore, such information should be reviewed and validated by healthcare professionals before being provided to patients. This study aims to evaluate the effect of an artificial intelligence-assisted patient education material delivered during the pre-suturing waiting period on pain and anxiety levels among patients with minor trauma in the emergency department. It is also expected that the educational material developed within the scope of this study may contribute to patient education and supportive care in emergency department settings.

title: MMedAgent-Plus: Scaling Multimodal Medical Agents across Modalities, Tasks and Workflows
desc: Medical workflows often require multiple interdependent analyses, but existing specialist and generalist AI models are not designed to coordinate them. We introduce MMedAgent-Plus, a multimodal medical tool-use agent that combines a vision-language planner with 18 leading specialist models spanning 12 tasks and 8 modalities. Through a unified tool interface, the planner selects specialists, executes them in sequence, and synthesizes responses grounded in their outputs. The planner is instruction-tuned on 208,928 samples from 32 public medical benchmarks, covering single- and multi-tool interactions across single and multiple rounds. We separately evaluate tool orchestration, response synthesis, and end-to-end execution on held-out samples. MMedAgent-Plus achieves tool-call accuracies of 91.0%, 98.1%, and 80.7% in single-tool multi-round, multi-tool multi-round, and multi-tool single-round settings, respectively. Given correct tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus achieves scores of 14.4-14.8 out of 15 for faithfulness, completeness, and conciseness across 600 evaluation samples. In end-to-end execution without pre-supplied tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus correctly invokes the required specialist in 90.6% of 350 evaluation cases spanning seven tasks. Its final-answer accuracy reaches 0.98, matching the dedicated leading specialist and exceeding the strongest baseline (0.28).

title: Cross-database adaptation of machine learning models for predicting sustained antibiotic exposure among patients with intracerebral hemorrhage in intensive care units
desc: BackgroundPatients with intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) in intensive care units (ICUs) frequently receive antibiotics early in critical illness. Such exposure reflects suspected infection, physiological deterioration, monitoring intensity, and clinical management and may vary across institutions and electronic health record databases. We evaluated target-domain adaptation for modeling sustained antibiotic exposure in critically ill patients with ICH. MethodsWe analyzed derived ICH cohorts from MIMIC-IV and the eICU Collaborative Research Database. MIMIC-IV included 2,024 ICU stays and served as the source cohort. The eICU cohort comprised 1,277 stays and was divided, at the ICU-stay level, into a development subset (766 stays) and a held-out evaluation subset (511 stays). The eICU outcome was sustained antibiotic exposure on at least two ICU days. Candidate models incorporated demographic, comorbidity, physiological, laboratory, neurologic, respiratory, temporal, and measurementprocess features. Timestamped observations for static and temporal tabular families were censored at the recorded first-antibiotic time when available, whereas the compact sequence component and explicit measurement-density features used the full first 24 hours. For base-model families using eICU development data, meta-learner inputs were generated by five-fold stratified cross-fitting. A 42-input L2-penalized logistic meta-learner combined 16 model probabilities with model-summary, clinical, availability, and measurement-density features. ResultsThe held-out eICU subset contained 48 positive outcomes (9.39%). The adapted ensemble achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.841 (95% CI 0.775-0.899) and an average precision (AP) of 0.540 (95% CI 0.399-0.676), with a Brier score of 0.063 and expected calibration error of 0.029. The MIMIC-IV source-only stack achieved an AUROC of 0.782; the paired AUROC difference was 0.059 (95% CI 0.003-0.112). In a separate patient-grouped five-fold out-of-fold sensitivity analysis of 503 linked eICU stays, AUROC was 0.807 (95% CI 0.691-0.910). ConclusionsTarget-domain adaptation improved held-out discrimination relative to a source-only stack for sustained antibiotic exposure. title: XGLASS: X-Ray, Gaze and Language Assisted Slice Sequencing for CT Volumes
desc: Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve remarkable performance on 2D medical images, such as X-rays or pathology images, while 3D VLMs that directly process CT/MRI volumes lag behind due to limited 3D training data and the predominance of 2D foundation architectures. To leverage powerful 2D VLMs for analyzing medical volumes, which contain hundreds of slices, it is therefore necessary to focus only on those few slices, which are diagnostically relevant. To enable such a prioritization, we propose XGLASS, a method that transfers medical expertise from 2D X-rays to 3D CT for task-aware slice prioritization. title: General Purpose AI for Public Data Analysis and Experimental Hypothesis Generation
desc: Public molecular datasets can support biological questions beyond those addressed in the original studies. We examined how general-purpose AI could help generate and investigate such questions through four complementary investigations. Interactive single-cell analysis identified Apelin signaling as a candidate for promoting mesendoderm differentiation of human pluripotent stem cells, although subsequent experiments did not establish an effect under the tested conditions. Autonomous analyses then searched public single-cell data for tumor antigens that could be targeted by engineered immune cells. Three multiple-myeloma runs shared 50 candidates and repeatedly recovered BCMA and CD38, whereas three pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma runs produced different exploratory results and nominated no target meeting their selection criteria. To examine whether published datasets could yield additional biological insights, we conducted two separate AI analyses of anonymized lung single-cell data without providing the original publication. One analysis was performed without information about the tissue type or disease status, while the other was provided with this information. Without tissue or disease information, the AI identified lung cell populations and inferred disease-associated tissue remodeling. The analyses also generated additional biological questions, eight of which showed statistical support in an independent patient dataset, including coordinated antioxidant-related expression across epithelial cell types and increased fibroblast CRYM expression. Finally, a broader public-data analysis integrated RNA expression, proteomics, CRISPR-based functional screening, and normal-tissue expression to prioritize 213 potential therapeutic targets for pancreatic cancer. Combining these measurements helped distinguish candidates with similar RNA evidence and assess their functional relevance and expression in normal tissues, although therapeutic selectivity remains to be established. Together, these investigations show how general-purpose AI can extend an experimental biologist's use of public data, generate testable hypotheses and identify biological relationships for further study. They also show why completing an analysis and obtaining a reproducible expression pattern are distinct from establishing an experimental or therapeutic effect.
